summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The national identity document has offered an "X" marker since 2021. Marriage equality has been available since 2010, and anti-discrimination protection rests on a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting adolescents' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, a measure reported elsewhere as DNU 62/2025, alongside a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the restriction illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention. The 2012 law remains formally in force, but activists told the Washington Blade in April 2025 that its guarantees are no longer being delivered in practice.

No Misiones-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. Interior provinces with little local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where the risk is real, so the absence of Misiones material reflects documentation capacity rather than demonstrated safety.

The documented picture is national and deteriorating. At least 227 hate crimes against LGBT+ people were recorded across Argentina in 2025, a 62% increase on the previous year and the worst total of the national observatory's ten recorded years, an average of one attack every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 142 of the 227 victims, or 62.5% of the tally.

Physical violence against bodily integrity made up 147 cases, 64.8% of the total, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers acting in public space, and the observatory attributes the surge to the national government's "cultural battle" against LGBTI+ people and to the surrounding hate discourse.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, and marks the position as deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

Trans activists interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation under the Milei government and said its policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

The February 2025 restriction on gender-affirming care bears on visitors travelling with transgender or gender-diverse minors, whose treatment options in Argentina have narrowed since the decree took effect.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and the 2012 Gender Identity Law was described by the United Nations as pioneering in the region. Both sit alongside a 2025 record year for recorded anti-LGBT+ hate crime, so formal legal standing and lived enforcement point in opposite directions.
localsOnly:
The Milei government eliminated the national Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity and dismissed transgender hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts; activists say the quota is no longer being implemented.

A decree of February 2025 governs the housing of transgender people in prisons, a measure affecting residents rather than visitors.

Anti-discrimination protection for residents rests on a combination of national law and the laws of individual provinces, and the scope of the provincial layer applicable in Misiones is not described in these sources.

National hate-crime monitoring is Buenos Aires-based and national in remit; residents of interior provinces such as Misiones appear in the tally only where a case is reported to it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Misiones-specific incidents, policing practice, or document-office behaviour is sourced here; whether Law 26.743 is delivered as written in Misiones registry offices is unresolved on these materials.

The observatory's 2025 figures are national and are not disaggregated by province in the source, so no Misiones share of the 227 recorded crimes can be stated.

The sources record an intention by legal experts to challenge the February 2025 decrees in court. Whether a court has ruled on them, and with what effect in Misiones, is unresolved and not sourced.

The activists' assessment that the Gender Identity Law is no longer guaranteed comes from interviews conducted in Buenos Aires and is not a measured finding about every province.

Outright International's negative assessments derive from its own country-overview methodology; the underlying provincial indicators, if any, are not published in these sources.
